listings.title: The Piraki Log Diary Of Captain Hempleman New Zealand Whaling  Published 1910
listings.body:
The Piraki Log Diary Of Captain Hempleman New Zealand Whaling History Anson Edition Oxford 1910

The Piraki Log - A significant early record of whaling activity settlement and coastal life around Banks Peninsula. The volume includes an introduction glossary illustrations and a detailed map which together provide context for the events described in the original manuscript. The diary was edited and published by F A Anson who served as chairman of the Akaroa County Council and who ensured that the manuscript was preserved and deposited in the museum at Christchurch. The book offers insight into the daily operations of a whaling station including provisions lists gear inventories slop accounts and the names of vessels and crew members associated with the station. The contents also include records of whales caught equipment lost and stores used across several years which makes the book a valuable resource for maritime historians and researchers studying early European activity in New Zealand. The map of Banks Peninsula included in the publication highlights bays headlands and Maori place names which adds geographical depth to the diary entries.The detailed lists and chronological entries provide a rare look at the logistics of nineteenth century whaling operations and the relationships between crew members vessels and the coastal environment. This edition is of interest to collectors of New Zealand maritime history those researching Banks Peninsula and anyone seeking original source material relating to early settlement and whaling.

The research focuses on the Omata Stockade and the Warea Redoubt, offering a detailed analysis of the fortifications and the living conditions during the New Zealand Wars. The text includes an introduction to the conflict within Taranaki and the specific role of these defensive structures. Technical data is provided regarding the history of the Omata Stockade, the excavation process, and a comprehensive study of recovered artefacts. Similarly, the work documents the surface evidence, excavation findings, and historical context of the Warea Redoubt.

The documentation serves as a critical archaeological and historical resource, utilizing physical evidence to reconstruct the daily realities of military life in 19th-century New Zealand. It provides precise details on the construction of earthworks and the material culture of the period through the analysis of site-specific findings. This volume is part of the New Zealand Archaeological Association Monograph series and represents a major contribution to the recorded history of Taranaki's military landscape.

This action-packed volume by Rex Forrester captures the wild era of helicopter hunting in New Zealand, chronicling the rise of airborne deer recovery and the rugged individuals who pioneered it. Readers are introduced to the development of the net gun, the dangers of strop hanging, and the realities of enemy gunfire. listings.body:
Life & Times Of 7 Brothers & 6 Siters In The Kauri Timber Days 

Foote Prints Among The Kauri is the story of the lives and times of seven brothers and six sisters, and the kauri timber industry around them.

In the 1890's, after milling at Whananaki and Maungatapere, near Whangarei, the partnership of Foote Bros felled and milled thousands of burnt and green kauri trees from the great Puhipuhi forest.

With their energy and innovation they paved the way for the use of steam-powered traction engines and log haulers in the Northland bush and led the establishment of the Whangarei Engineering Company.

Sisters Foote were amongst New Zealand's earliest nurses, playing a leading role during the formative years of the profession and through World War I.

The family's early days in Newfoundland, emigration to New Zealand in a small brigantine, and the establishment of one of the country's first steam-powered saw mills, near the Manukau Heads.
The lives of the thirteen children of William and Elizabeth Foote are traced around Northland as they touch Whananaki and Whangaruru, Maungatapere and Whangarei, Herekino and Hokianga. Fred and Will Foote are followed across USA and Canada as they journey back to their roots in Newfoundland at the turn of the century.

The book looks back from today at changing attitudes to the exploitation of the kauri forests and guides the reader to the sites of some early mills and the signs from the past.

Bill Haigh, a civil engineer living in Kerikeri, is a great-grandson of one of the seven Foote brothers.

NORSEWOOD. To many just a name on a signpost somewhere in Hawkes Bay on the main Napier Wellington highway pointing to the distant blue Ruahines. To others a town now off the main highway, "Ghost Town;" a town that was

But the ghosts of the past that haunt this small Scandinavian town were very real people as this book testifies, people who set out from Norway, Sweden and Denmark to brave unknown hardships and dangers, people who with fortitude, an unquenchable spirit and an unfailing sense of humour in the face of obstacles at last set up their homes in this little Town in the Southern Hemisphere.

Theirs is a fascinating story. Together they faced devastating bushfires which overnight almost completely wiped out their homes, churches and store. Faith was the very root of existence. Bound together by their dependence on each other for sheer survival. there emerged a hard-working, closely-knit community, ready to share their joys and sorrows alike, facing their difficulties with a wiry humour that rescued them from the most desperate situations. It is this Norsewood that Archie Andersen

reveals - a highly individual Scandinavian town. Himself of Danish pioneering stock - his father owned a sawmill in this heavily bushed area Archie Andersen was brought up to the stories of these early struggles and has always evinced a keen interest in them. listings.title: An illustrated history of the Mount Rochfort Railway and the Denniston Incline
listings.body:
Coaling from the clouds
 R.J. Meyer

An illustrated brief history of the Mount Rochfort railway and the Denniston Incline


ONE OF WESTLAND’S MOST dramatic engineering marvels, the Denniston Incline, is the main feature of Westport’s coalmining museum, Coaltown. In 1859, surveyor John Rochfort first discovered coal in a small creek 14km north of Westport. However, it was not until 1860 that Dr Julius von Haast found seams of prized bituminous coal high on the fog-shrouded plateau which bears Rochfort’s name.

Before it could be used to power the industrial machinery of last century, the coal had to be transported down from the plateau. The ingenious construction of the Dennis-ton Incline in 1878-79 overcame the problem by using the coal’s very height above sea level to shift it to the railhead.

Packtrack to Highway provides a warm, honest, and firsthand chronological account of a pioneering style of life on the early frontiers. This volume serves as a vital historical and social record for the West Coast and Wellington regions, documenting the immense physical hardships, high-stakes gold mining operations, and raw determination required to carve out a living along the remote back-country tracks and diggings of the nineteenth century.

The narrative holds significant historical, local, and genealogical value, capturing the lived experiences of a gold miner's son who witnessed the historic 1879 gold rush to Kumara. The text methodically chronicles the atmospheric reality of early mining settlements—complete with cosmopolitan crowds, lively dance halls, and streets illuminated by kerosene lanterns on poles. From early childhood memories of sluicing claims to adolescent years spent digging tunnel tail races alone through the night, the author paints a vivid picture of the goldfields, including the thrill of uncovering substantial nuggets for early employers. 

Beyond the West Coast diggings, this publication follows the author's adventures as a young man exploring the northern frontier settlements of the Wellington province. It preserves detailed descriptions of working alongside surveying parties, packing stores down dense forest tracks, driving coaching teams between Feilding and Kimbolton, hunting wild pigs near Karioi, and mustering wild horses on the tussock plains south of Ruapehu. It stands as an invaluable reference for regional historians and researchers tracking the social development, early surveying expeditions, and rugged transport networks of early New Zealand.

listings.title: Whanganui Historical Record Vol 27 Wanganui Land Purchase Journal Records 1846
listings.body:
Wanganui Historical Record Mag Vol 27 May 1996 

50  pages 


This book presents regional historical documentation, focusing on the mid-nineteenth century colonial land dealings in the district. It features transcriptions and historical analyses of early primary source records from 1846.

Contents:
* Editorial 
* Donald McLean and the "Wanganui Land Question"

* Illustrations: Along Taupo Quay, G A Sherriff after J A Gilfillan
* Ngapara 
* Maketu 
* Te Matoha 
* Mitta kingi
* Kanawa 

This book provides specific regional history data drawn from the 1846 journal entries of Donald McLean regarding his efforts to purchase Wanganui land. The contents include material extracted from the typescript of Rev. Richard Taylor's journal for the same period. It covers historical interactions involving William Spain, J. J. Symonds, and T. S. Forsaith, alongside context on regional events such as the death of Te Heuheu at Te Rapa near Tokaanu. It serves as a factual resource for research into regional land transactions, early settlement, and iwi history along the Whanganui River.

Keywords: Whanganui History, Wanganui Land Question, Donald McLean, Richard Taylor, Land Purchase, Colonial History, Taupo Quay, Regional History Journal, Whanganui River History
